partial_case.facts: The resident lives in the property with his wife, who is vulnerable and requires support and personal care. He reported that the home was cold and that he faced high energy bills, which he struggled to pay. The resident contacted his landlord on 24 October 2023, asking for loft and wall insulation because he was struggling with high energy costs. He said he was paying around £300 per month to his energy provider and was still in debt. The landlord inspected the property on 6 November 2023 and found the loft had 250mm insulation, which met requirements, but noted the resident's CCTV installation had disturbed it. The landlord explained wall insulation programmes were large-scale, costly, and on hold due to budget pressures. The resident has since purchased this property.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not go far enough to demonstrate the property provided a reasonable level of thermal comfort. It did not support or signpost the resident for help with his increasing energy costs. The landlord's approach was not customer focused.
There is no evidence that the landlord satisfied itself that the property provided a reasonable level of thermal comfort or offered practical support to help the resident manage high energy costs.

The landlord's complaint process was an opportunity to resolve the matter in line with the Ombudsman's Dispute Resolution Principles. It should have taken ownership and acted in a customer-focused way but instead concentrated on what it claimed the resident had done rather than addressing the concerns raised.

evidence: Resident’s complaint/request that he contacted the landlord on 24 October 2023 asking for loft and wall insulation because of high energy costs and cold conditions.

Landlord’s stage 1 response said it inspected the property on 6 November 2023, found 250mm loft insulation, noted CCTV disturbance, and refused wall insulation for budget, planning and practical reasons.
Landlord’s stage 2 response repeated that the property was suitably insulated, referred to CCTV displacement, and said there were no plans for an external wall insulation programme.
The Ombudsman noted there was no copy of the inspection report and no evidence that the landlord checked thermal efficiency or arranged a heat loss survey.
The decision referred to EPC material: EPC rating D, 250mm loft insulation, walls rated poor, and a recommendation for cavity wall insulation.
partial_case.facts: The resident lived in the property with his wife, who was vulnerable and required support and personal care; he reported the home was cold and that he struggled with high energy bills. The resident later purchased the property. The complaint concerned the landlord’s response to a request for loft and wall insulation, the impact of poor energy efficiency on energy bills, and complaint handling. On 12 January 2024, the resident said he had contacted the landlord on 24 October 2023 asking for loft and wall insulation because he was struggling with high energy costs, had not received a response, and continued to experience draughts. The landlord issued a stage 1 response on 24 January 2024 summarising its inspection, the 250mm loft insulation, disturbance by CCTV installation, and its position that wall insulation could not be offered. The resident escalated the complaint on 24 January 2024, saying he believed the landlord was responsible for energy efficiency and high energy costs, and disputing the landlord’s account of the loft insulation and external insulation position. The landlord issued a stage 2 response on 12 February 2024, confirming its view that the property was suitably insulated, referring to CCTV displacement, and saying there were no plans for an external wall insulation programme. On referral to the Ombudsman, the resident said the property had no wall insulation and very old loft insulation, that he paid around £270 per month for gas and electricity while still living in a cold house, and that he wanted energy-efficiency improvements, compensation, planning permission for external insulation and replacement loft insulation.

key_reasoning_quotes.text: The landlord did not go far enough to demonstrate the property provided a reasonable level of thermal comfort. It did not support or signpost the resident for help with his increasing energy costs. The landlord’s approach was not customer focused

We do not have a copy of the inspection report, so we cannot confirm what checks were carried out or if the landlord’s actions after the inspection met its obligations under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 and the Decent Homes Standard.
Given the resident’s concerns about cold and his wife’s known vulnerabilities, the landlord should have checked thermal efficiency or arranged a heat loss survey. There is no evidence this happened.
The absence of such an assessment was a failing by the landlord.

It would have been reasonable for the landlord to refer the resident to these resources, provided practical guidance or signposted the resident to its website. Doing so would have shown that the landlord supported the resident and took steps to help manage energy costs.

Overall, the landlord did not have to provide external wall insulation because this is an improvement rather than a repair under the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985. However, there is no evidence that the landlord satisfied itself that the property provided a reasonable level of thermal comfort or offered practical support to help the resident manage high energy costs.
Taken together, these failings amount to maladministration.
